content: MUST-CHECK: archiveOlderThan in scripts/lib/store.ts compares e.ts < cutoffTs (strict less-than). An entry created in the same second as an archive --days 0 call will NOT be archived because its ts equals (not less than) the cutoff. Tests exercising --days 0 or small day windows must seed entries with an explicit past ts (e.g. now - 3600) via direct JSONL write, not rely on wall-clock timing.

CLI numeric flags (kb.ts --days/--since/--limit) must be validated with a digits-only regex (all-digit test) BEFORE calling Number(raw). Number() alone accepts floats, hex (0x10), exponents (1e3), trailing dots (3.), and coerces empty/whitespace strings to 0 -- all of which are dangerous when the value feeds a cutoff calculation (e.g. archive --days). The single shared validator (parseNonNegInt in scripts/kb.ts) is the only call site for all three numeric flags.

MUST-CHECK: In scripts/kb.ts parseFlags, a flag with no consumable value stores boolean true, not a string. Guards like `typeof flags.x === "string"` silently skip validation and fall through to defaults for that flag, which is dangerous for destructive commands (e.g. archive --days with a swallowed/empty value defaulted to 90 instead of erroring). Always add an explicit `if (flags.x === true) { error; return 1; }` guard before the string-type check for any flag whose absence has a meaningfully different behavior than a present-but-empty value.

MUST-CHECK: A test that only asserts the post-condition of a destructive/cleanup operation (e.g. "store is empty after archive") is vacuously true if the seed data never landed (wrong file path, bad fixture). Always assert the pre-state (seed count before the call) and/or a positive post-state (e.g. archive now contains N entries), not just the negative absence.

MUST-CHECK: the drawbar kb store's active file is knowledge.jsonl (archive: knowledge.archive.jsonl), per storePaths() in scripts/lib/store.ts. When hand-building a shell harness to verify archive/compact behavior, seeding a file named active.jsonl (or any other guess) leaves the real store EMPTY, so every destructive command reports success against nothing and the store-preserved assertion passes vacuously. Verified this the hard way while reviewing PCO-339: an 8-vector wipe test appeared to pass with the store intact, but the store was never populated. Always seed via the real filename, or via ensureDir(dir).active, and assert a non-zero pre-state count before the destructive call.

MUST-CHECK: scripts/kb.ts compact uses flags["dry-run"] === true, so `kb compact --dry-run 1` binds the string "1", the === true test is false, and a REAL compaction runs while the operator believes they are previewing. This is the mirror image of the PCO-339 --days bug: there a boolean-where-string-expected failed open, here a string-where-boolean-expected fails open. Data-preserving (losers go to the archive, recoverable via recall --all) and pre-existing, so it was left out of PCO-339 scope. Belongs to PCO-340/S2, whose LD5 mandates flag type enforcement in BOTH directions. The same latent shape exists for recall --all and --json, but those fail in the narrowing direction and are not an exposure.

MUST-CHECK: when writing tests that assert bm25(kb) ranking order for OR-joined multi-token FTS5 queries, do not assume the entry matching more distinct query tokens always ranks first, or that ts breaks ties in the direction you expect. bm25 favors rows matching rarer terms (lower doc frequency) over rows matching more common terms, even if another row matches more total tokens. Verify actual ranking with a throwaway script against the real fixture before hardcoding expected order in a test.

MUST-CHECK: FTS5 bm25() ranking sorts by term rarity (IDF), not by how many query tokens a row matches. A row matching one rare token can outrank a row matching two common tokens (near-zero IDF each). Do not name/comment tests as "matches more tokens ranks higher" -- isolate rarity vs token-count as independent variables when writing ranking fixtures, or the test will pass for the wrong reason.

fts5 bm25 clamps a non-positive IDF to 1e-6 rather than 0. Even when every matched term is common (df == N), bm25 stays a strictly ordered function of term frequency and document length at a tiny magnitude — it never actually ties, so ts DESC is never reached as a general fallback for common-term queries. ts DESC only breaks bit-identical bm25 values, which requires structurally symmetric rows (same doc length, same df/tf per matched term). Do not describe common-term bm25 behavior as falling back to recency.

MUST-CHECK: a bm25 test claiming to prove term-rarity dominance (rare token beats a doc matching two common tokens) must hold document length EQUAL between the two compared rows, or document-length normalization (shorter docs score better) can produce the same ranking for the wrong reason, and a one-word edit to a fixture string can silently flip the result. Verify by sweeping the non-length-controlled document's word count across a wide range (we used 1-20 words) and confirming the ranking never flips before trusting the test.

MUST-CHECK: when hand-writing a probe to verify a test's behavior outside the test runner, replicate the ENTIRE fixture, including whatever beforeEach seeds. A partial fixture can silently invert the conclusion. Hit twice in one session: (1) seeded a store file named active.jsonl when the real one is knowledge.jsonl, so a destructive-command check passed against an empty store (see [[kb-store-active-file-is-knowledge-jsonl]]); (2) probed a bm25 ranking claim with only the 4 entries the test appends, omitting the 3 the describe block's beforeEach seeds -- N=4 instead of N=7 changed every document frequency and produced the OPPOSITE result, wrongly clearing a reviewer finding that was in fact correct. Corollary for FTS/bm25 specifically: document frequency is a property of the whole table, so ANY entry present changes ranking. Re-probe against real conditions before accepting or rejecting a ranking claim.

MUST-CHECK: before moving a story to In Progress and dispatching an implementer, verify the paths in the story ## Files section are actually WRITABLE from this session, not merely readable. A directory can be listed as an additional working directory, be owned by the user, show drwxr-xr-x with no ACLs, and still return EPERM (Operation not permitted) on every write -- the harness sandbox profile is applied at process spawn and disabling the sandbox does NOT lift it. Cheap probe: touch <dir>/.probe && rm <dir>/.probe, run as part of the step 3 prerequisite gate. It costs one command and saves burning an implementer agent against a read-only tree. The failure mode is easy to misdiagnose because it surfaces as a git ref error (cannot lock ref ... unable to create directory) rather than a permissions error, so it reads like a bad branch name. Also beware: the shell tool persists its working directory between calls, so a probe can silently run against the wrong repo after an earlier cd -- always probe with absolute paths.

PCO-345 was replanned 2026-07-28: no story writes to the legacy operator workspace. The epic is a port OUT of that workspace into this plugin repo, and the workspace is additionally read-only to the agent environment (EPERM on every write). Consequences: S1/PCO-346 (a throwaway shell shim on the legacy copies) is CANCELLED -- its only value was protecting a live copy that will keep running, which is no longer true; S2/PCO-347 becomes the first story and ports the files, scrubbed, in one commit; the CodeRabbit review-gate defect is closed by S4/PCO-349 as a tested module. Deleting the legacy copies and re-homing workspace-specific reasoning are MANUAL operator cleanup, not story steps. Parent Locked 1 reversed, Locked 3 and 20 de-scoped, AC L1 withdrawn. Detail on the specific defect lives in the Linear issues, deliberately not here -- see [[drawbar-repo-is-public-scrub-before-porting]] for why a public KB must carry rules, not exemplars.

Grep-preservation tests for a Locked rule should anchor on the exact operative sentence (e.g. the imperative bullet), not just a section header — a header survives many mutations that gut the rule underneath it. For multi-sentence sections (e.g. story-lead section 4), assert several distinct sentences so a partial deletion still trips the test.
Reconciled plugin.json/package.json version drift by taking plugin.json 0.1.4 (the more-advanced, plugin-manifest source of truth) and bumping package.json to match, rather than the reverse.

MUST-CHECK: this plugin repo is PUBLIC (verify with gh repo view --json visibility before assuming). Anything ported into it from a private workspace must first be scrubbed of: org and repo names, CI workflow filenames, deploy and production trigger surfaces, live PR numbers and commit shas, issue-tracker team prefixes and issue ids, branch naming conventions, status-lattice names unique to one board, internal domain-model terms, and absolute filesystem paths. Public git history is permanent, so a later scrub story does NOT remove the content -- any plan that sequences a verbatim private-to-public port ahead of its de-hardcoding story is defective by construction, however reviewable the two-step looks. Fold the scrub into the porting commit. Two corollaries learned the hard way: (1) the scrub must cover the TEST file and the KB JSONL, not just the ported docs -- a leak-regression denylist that names the forbidden strings, and a KB entry that cites its own examples, both re-publish exactly what was removed; write shape-based rules and rule-only lessons instead. (2) grep the WHOLE working tree, not the subset of directories you think the story touched.

MUST-CHECK: before removing a hardcoded environment anchor during a de-hardcoding pass, ask what that anchor is currently GATING, not merely what it hardcodes. An anchor that pins a command to one specific repo reads like pure hardcoding to parameterize away, but it can be the only thing making an unfixed vulnerability elsewhere in the same runbook unreachable by third parties. Three consequences: (1) replace such an anchor with a FAIL-CLOSED placeholder -- unconfigured must mean REFUSE, never allow-all -- and test the closed path explicitly; (2) sequence the story that fixes the underlying vulnerability BEFORE the story that removes its accidental gate, even if the original plan had the reverse dependency; (3) recognise the limit of a config-based replacement: an env var an operator simply sets is an opt-in, not an access control, so it does not preserve the by-construction unreachability the hardcoded anchor gave you. If genuine containment is needed in the gap, add a gate that naming a repo cannot satisfy. Related trap: substituting a placeholder like <TEAM>-#### into executable bash UNQUOTED makes the shell parse < and > as redirection and assign an EMPTY string -- silently converting a downstream substring guard into match-anything. Always quote placeholders in shipped shell, and assert the variable is non-empty before any guard depends on it.

MUST-CHECK: when extracting a runbook bash snippet (from a .md doc) and spawning it to test a guard/refusal path, capture and assert against combined stdout+stderr, not stderr alone. Plain `echo "FATAL: ..."` writes to stdout by default; a test that only reads stderr sees an empty string on a correctly-failing guard and misreports the assertion as broken rather than the guard.

MUST-CHECK: expect(a.version).toBe(b.version) across two independently-sourced JSON files is vacuously true if both version keys are ever absent (undefined === undefined). Always assert a positive shape (e.g. a semver regex) on at least one side before the cross-file equality check.

MUST-CHECK: when writing a test that asserts a scrubbed/ported doc file contains no leaked private identifiers, the test itself becomes permanent public history — a FORBIDDEN array of literal org names/team prefixes/CI filenames just relocates the leak into the test file instead of eliminating it. Use shape-based regex rules (issue-id shape, config-filename shape, absolute-home-path shape, owner/repo slug shape) instead of naming the actual identifiers, and describe each rule's own examples in comments without a literal string that matches its own shape -- once the test scans itself, a literal example in a rule's comment trips that same rule. A trigger-line-scoped exemption on the slug rule (only checking lines that also mention a GitHub remote/CLI operation) failed open: a leaked slug on a line with no trigger word went undetected while the suite stayed green. Replaced with: scan every line, and exempt by a small reviewed VALUE allowlist of the specific benign non-placeholder matches already present, not by line shape. Trade-off: loses detection of a bare unstructured codename, which is an accepted cost for structured identifiers. Verify each rule both directions against a scratch copy (real violation goes RED; the placeholder forms actually used in the scrubbed docs, e.g. <TEAM>-###, <ci-workflow>.yml, <org>/<repo>, do not false-positive) before trusting the suite green.

MUST-CHECK: when a leak-regression test is extended to scan its OWN source file (or any file that must legitimately describe/implement the forbidden shapes), a uniform rule-list applied to a uniform file-list breaks in two ways: (1) a rule comment giving a concrete illustrative example that happens to match the shape it defines (a team-prefix-plus-digits string, or a real-looking config filename) trips its own rule once self-scanned -- describe the shape in words only, with no literal instance that matches it, even inside this very KB entry; (2) a rule implemented via a literal string match trips on the file that defines it, since the rule source necessarily contains the literal it is checking for -- exclude the rule's own defining file from that rule's scope rather than trying to make it pass. Also: a slug-shaped (owner/repo) rule that scans every line is fine on terse runbook docs but explodes into false positives on prose-heavy files (KB entries, test comments) full of ordinary word-slash-word pairs -- scope that rule to the terse docs only rather than growing an unbounded allowlist.

When a leak-regression rule matches concrete issue-id shape (uppercase team prefix, hyphen, 2+ digits) and the scan is extended to files that legitimately cite this repos own public issue tracker (e.g. every KB entrys issue field), exclude that ONE known-public prefix via a negative lookahead rather than dropping the rule or allowlisting every id. Verified the prefix is genuinely already public by checking git log on main for real commit messages citing it before relying on this.

MUST-CHECK: superseding a knowledge entry (re-adding an existing key) does NOT erase the previous text -- the store moves the prior version into the archive JSONL alongside the active one. So redacting a leaked entry by re-adding a clean version of it leaves the ORIGINAL, unredacted text on disk. Worse, that archive file is created on demand, is not covered by the memory directory gitignore (which only ignores the index db), and starts life untracked -- so it is one sweeping git add away from committing exactly the text the redaction removed. Hit while scrubbing four entries in a public repo: all four active entries verified clean, while the archive silently held all four originals. Guards: (1) after any supersede intended as a redaction, check whether the archive now exists and what it holds; (2) include the archive in whatever leak scan covers the active store, tolerating its absence explicitly so a skip is visible rather than a silent pass; (3) remember the CLI has no delete verb -- removing an entry means editing the JSONL source of truth directly and running reindex, and note that a supersede would recreate the archive you just cleaned.

MUST-CHECK: a test runner name filter (bun test -t, jest -t, vitest -t) is a REGEX, not a literal substring. A filter copied from a test title containing parentheses, brackets, +, ?, or . will silently match ZERO tests and the runner reports 0 fail -- which is indistinguishable from a pass. Any verification harness that shells out to a filtered test run must assert a NON-ZERO test count actually ran before trusting the pass/fail verdict, exactly as an assertion over a spy must first prove the spy was called. This inverted a conclusion during PCO-347: a mutation harness checking that seven preservation tests each fail when their rule is deleted reported one of them as VACUOUS, when in fact the filter (which contained literal parens) had selected no tests at all and the test was fine. Nearly filed a false defect against correct code. Parse the runner summary for both the pass and fail counts, sum them, and require the expected number.

MUST-CHECK: when adding a guard whose job is to stop a specific defect recurring, prove it RED against the ACTUAL historical input that caused the defect -- not a plausible reconstruction. A synthetic example is written by the same mind that wrote the guard, so it tends to share the guard hidden assumptions and passes for the wrong reason. Concretely on PCO-347: a leak-detection rule only inspected lines containing certain trigger words. A hand-written violation happened to include one of those triggers, so the rule caught it and the guard looked sound. The real historical leak line contained none of them and sailed straight through -- the guard was fail-open on the one input it existed to catch, and only an adversarial reviewer re-injecting the verbatim original found it. Keep the offending input verbatim (in the ticket, a fixture, or the commit that removed it) so the guard can be tested against the real thing, and treat a guard proven only against synthetic input as unproven.

MUST-CHECK: never use git stash to get a clean base-branch state for a comparison probe (e.g. is this typecheck error pre-existing on main). stash -u sweeps the uncommitted work under review -- including untracked new files -- out of the tree, and if the probe then errors or the session is interrupted, the work looks lost. Hit while verifying an implementer report during PCO-347: a stash intended to isolate a pre-existing build error silently removed the entire story diff, recovered only because stash pop was run immediately afterward. Use a throwaway worktree of the base ref instead (git worktree add <tmp> <base>), run the probe there, then remove it -- the working tree under review is never touched. Same rule applies to git checkout of a base ref, and to any clean-tree operation performed for measurement rather than for the work itself.

For PCO-349: implemented the CodeRabbit completion predicate as a single pure function coderabbitVerdict({headSha, statuses}) in scripts/lib/coderabbit.ts, with a separate injected-Runner fetch layer (fetchPrHeadSha/fetchCodeRabbitStatuses/checkPr) so gh is only ever touched by one real-runner closure at the CLI entry point. Only agents/drawbar-story-lead.md §7 actually calls the script via `bun run .../coderabbit.ts verdict --repo --pr` and parses JSON with jq. commands/drawbar-ship.md does NOT call it -- it only names the module in its preflight comment and in the Appendix amendment prose (corrected from an earlier version of this entry that wrongly claimed both files call it). Neither call site reimplements the (state, description) allowlist in bash. A grep-based single-implementation-site test must match the executable comparison shape (e.g. description === "Review completed"), not the raw phrase, because the phrase legitimately also appears as measured evidence in an Appendix and as inline expected-output comments at call sites -- and per PCO-349's fix-pass review, that grep must scan the whole repo (not a fixed file list) and match jq's `==` shape too, not just TS `===`, or a hand-rolled bash/jq duplicate slips past silently.

When a story's tests assert on the current content of a shipped runbook .md file (e.g. a preservation/anti-regression grep test), you can still show a genuine RED run without hand-reverting by hand: `git stash push -- <the two md files>` restores the pre-fix committed content, run the test suite and confirm the expected tests fail for the right reason, then `git stash pop` to restore the fix and confirm green. This is safe because the tree is otherwise untracked/uncommitted work in other files (new .ts files, other test edits) which the stash leaves alone when you name the paths explicitly. For a historical regression fixture (the ACTUAL pre-fix bash predicate, not a hand reconstruction), `git show HEAD:<path>` reads the last-committed blob even after the working tree has already been edited (as long as you have not committed yet) -- extract the exact function text from that blob rather than retyping it from the story brief.

MUST-CHECK: a regression guard that pins pre-fix historical behavior must not resolve that history via a moving ref like `git show HEAD:<file>` inside the test itself. HEAD is exactly the ref the fix commit will update, so the guard passes only in the uncommitted window before the fix lands and goes red on its own PR the moment it is committed. Pin the historical text as a checked-in fixture (extracted once, at review time, from the specific historical commit sha via `git show <sha>:<file>`) with the source path + sha recorded as a provenance comment, so the fixture stays frozen regardless of where HEAD later points. Caught empirically by cloning the repo, copying the full working-tree fixture, committing, and re-running the suite — the failure only shows up post-commit, so a same-working-tree run alone cannot catch it.

MUST-CHECK: an Array.prototype.sort comparator that subtracts two Date#getTime() values (b - a) silently returns NaN whenever either timestamp is unparseable or empty, and a NaN comparator result does not mean 0 by spec -- relative order for that element becomes implementation-defined. In an allowlist-style verdict function (fail-closed philosophy), this lets a malformed/empty updated_at on a completed status win the latest-wins comparison ahead of a genuinely newer non-completed status, flipping ok:false to ok:true. Fix: never subtract two possibly-NaN times; convert unparseable/empty timestamps to -Infinity (oldest, never latest) via a helper, then compare with > / === (not subtraction) so two -Infinity values do not themselves subtract to NaN. Reachable in practice whenever the fetch layer coerces a missing field to empty string rather than throwing.

MUST-CHECK: fixing a NaN/-Infinity sort-comparator bug (see nan-comparator-sort-order-is-undefined) is not sufficient on its own -- once malformed timestamps are coerced to -Infinity, a genuine tie among valid, well-formed timestamps at the same second becomes routine (GitHub statuses have second resolution), and Array.prototype.sort is stable, so sorted[0] silently degrades to whatever order the array arrived in. In a latest-wins allowlist verdict, do not pick an arbitrary element from a tied group. Instead: compute the max timestamp, collect all entries tied at that max, and require every tied entry to independently satisfy the allowlist before returning ok:true; if the max itself is -Infinity (all candidates unparseable), disqualify outright rather than picking any of them. Caught by reproducing both array orderings of a same-second tie and asserting they produce the identical (refusing) verdict.

MUST-CHECK: the one real (non-injected) Runner closure at a CLI entry point (Locked-5 style pure-function-plus-injected-runner design) must wrap its Bun.spawnSync/spawn call in try/catch and return a fail-closed {code, stdout} on failure, never let the exception propagate uncaught. A missing binary on PATH (e.g. gh absent) throws ENOENT from spawnSync -- uncaught, this crashes the whole process with a stack trace to stderr and empty stdout, which downstream bash driving the CLI (VERDICT=$(bun run ...)) cannot distinguish from the tool just being slow: it silently retries/waits out a full deadline instead of failing fast. Pair with an explicit unreadable-verdict branch in the bash caller (case on $OK: true|false is fine, anything else parks immediately with a distinct diagnostic string) so infra failures are diagnosable within one loop iteration, not conflated with TIMEOUT an hour later.

A single-implementation-site regression test (this predicate/config exists in exactly one place) must grep the whole repo, not a fixed file list, and must match every syntax a duplicate could plausibly use (e.g. jqs == as well as TSs ===) -- a fixed file list plus a language-specific regex both silently miss a duplicate landing in a new file or a different language (bash/jq vs TS). Scope the scan to runbook/implementation surfaces (commands/, agents/, skills/, scripts/ -- broadened from scripts/lib/ so a duplicate landing anywhere else under scripts/ is not invisible) and exclude test files: a test file legitimately constructs dozens of literal fixture objects containing the exact phrase being scanned for, which is not an implementation site and would make an allowlist churn on every unrelated test edit. Key the allowlist on (file, TRIMMED matched-line CONTENT), never (file, line number): a line-number key breaks on any line-shifting edit anywhere above an allowlisted occurrence in that file (a one-line insert/delete elsewhere in the same file shifts the number with nothing wrong), and the failure message this produces is actively misleading -- it reads as new duplicate predicate or broken grep, not not the line moved. Use a Map<key,count> MULTISET, not a Set: a pure content key without counting would let a genuine second, identical copy of an allowlisted line silently pass (both instances share one key), which the old line-number Set caught only by accident (the two copies naturally land on different line numbers). Content-keying is also strictly stronger against a different mutation: editing an allowlisted line to weaken it changes its content, so it no longer matches its allowlist key and fails loudly -- a line-number key stays silent on that edit. Replace any line-number-pinned vacuity/non-vacuity guard the same way (assert on content, e.g. a line containing the known-good implementation, not a specific line number). Proven by inserting the literal hand-rolled duplicate a reviewer used and confirming the test goes red, by a real line-shifting edit that leaves the suite green, and by weakening an allowlisted line and confirming the suite goes red.

MUST-CHECK: array-form Bun.spawnSync (no shell:true) rules out command injection, but does not rule out endpoint injection -- an unvalidated repo/pr-shaped argument reaching a REST path template (e.g. repos/${repo}/pulls/${pr}) can redirect the request at a different resource if it carries .. or extra / segments, even though no shell ever parses it. This matters most when the argument is agent-held state sourced from a public/attacker-reachable input (a PR number on a public repo). Validate shape (e.g. digits-only for a numeric id, owner/repo slug shape for a repo) at both the CLI boundary (refuse with non-zero exit and no stdout output at all, not even a JSON ok:false object -- a caller grepping stdout for a verdict must never see one synthesized from unvalidated input) and again inside the pure function callers might invoke directly, skipping the CLI.

A guard field (e.g. a stale_sha check) that is stamped by the caller from the same value used to fetch the data can never fire -- it always trivially matches, and a field comment claiming protection is aspirational. Reading the field from the API payload instead gives it independent information so the guard can actually catch a caller reusing a stale/cached array. But if the real endpoint payload does not carry that field at all (verified against GitHubs actual statuses-list response shape, which has no per-entry sha), a naive payload-preferred-else-fallback MERGE lets the untrusted payload value overwrite the trusted URL-scoped one -- which means untrusted data can SATISFY the guard, not just fail it (a caller who fetches statuses for one sha and evaluates them against a different headSha is masked if the payload happens to carry the new sha). The correct shape is CONJUNCTION, not fallback-on-absence-else-merge: keep the URL-scoped value in its own trusted field always, read the payload sha into a SEPARATE optional field, and require both to agree (trusted===expected AND (untrusted===undefined OR untrusted===expected)). That way the untrusted payload field can only ever tighten the guard (add a reason to refuse), never loosen it -- while still preserving production correctness for the real endpoint, which never populates the untrusted field at all.

When a fail-closed verdict function computes a latest-status winner (max timestamp, disqualify on tie/unparseable), an actionable sub-reason (e.g. rate_limited vs the generic not_completed) must be checked in EVERY branch that can return the generic reason -- the single-winner branch, the tie branch, and the disqualified/all-unparseable branch -- not just the one the original fix targeted. Adding a fail-closed tie-break (Critical 1) and only wiring the actionable-reason check into the pre-existing single-winner branch left the tie and disqualified branches silently degrading rate_limited into not_completed, which is invisible to a caller that only asserts ok===false and defeats the whole point of having a distinguishable reason (a caller parks immediately on rate_limited but polls the full deadline on not_completed). Test each branch by asserting the SPECIFIC reason, not just ok===false.

A bash `: "${VAR:?msg}"` fail-closed guard inside a loop/fence is NOT proven by the suite staying green when it is replaced with `true` -- that only shows a hole exists. Prove the guard itself by running the real extracted fence with VAR genuinely unset in the child process env (Bun.spawn env fully REPLACES the childs environment rather than merging with the parents, so omitting the key from the env object reliably leaves it unset regardless of the test runners own process env) and asserting non-zero exit plus the specific `:?` message text, never STATUS=ready/success. `${VAR:?msg}` aborts a non-interactive shell unconditionally on an unset/null VAR, independent of `set -e` -- a harness can rely on that.

A poll loop that distinguishes domain-not-ready (e.g. CodeRabbit still reviewing) from an infrastructure failure (e.g. gh missing, a transient 502) must not treat a WELL-FORMED but failure-shaped verdict (e.g. {ok:false,reason:fetch_failed}) the same as an unparseable one. An unparseable-output guard (a case statement on OK true|false) does not catch this, because fetch_failed is perfectly parseable JSON -- it just silently falls through to the ordinary poll-until-deadline path, indistinguishable from CodeRabbit hasnt finished yet until the full deadline elapses. Fix: track consecutive occurrences of the specific infra-failure reason across loop iterations and park with a DISTINCT diagnostic (not the generic TIMEOUT) once a small bound (e.g. 3) is exceeded, resetting the counter on any other reason -- a transient failure is worth a retry, a persistently broken gate is not. Test with a fast-forwarded loop (stub `sleep` as a no-op alongside the fake binary under test) and a SHORT deadline, so the pre-fix behavior (silently burning the whole duration) is observable in a bounded test.

MUST-CHECK: a proof of the form "the suite passes with <tool> absent from PATH" is invalid if the scrubbed PATH also hides the test runner. env PATH=/nonexistent bun test does not prove gh is unneeded -- it fails with env: bun: No such file or directory, which an agent can report as a pass because no test failure is printed. Two correct forms, and run BOTH: (1) PATH set to only the runner directory (env -i PATH=$(dirname $(command -v bun)) HOME=$HOME bun test <file>) proves the unit file needs nothing else; (2) PATH with the normal toolchain but the one target binary removed, verified by asserting command -v <tool> actually fails in that PATH, proves the FULL suite tolerates its absence. Form (1) alone will red-herring any test that legitimately shells out to git/grep/bash. As the verifying lead, re-run a claimed absence proof yourself rather than accepting the pasted output -- the broken form and the real form produce output that looks similar at a glance.

MUST-CHECK: when mutation-testing with a scripted find/replace (perl -pi, sed), a pattern that fails to MATCH produces an unmutated tree that passes -- indistinguishable in the output from a genuine surviving mutant, and it points the reviewer at a nonexistent test gap. Hit twice in one session: patterns written against code that had since been renamed (Math.max -> reduce) or restructured from one line into a block. Always assert the mutation actually landed (grep the mutated file for the new text, or diff against the source) BEFORE concluding a mutant survived. Corollary for the opposite result: a mutant that genuinely survives is not automatically a test gap -- check for an EQUIVALENT mutant, where an earlier guard makes the mutated branch unreachable. Prove equivalence by removing that guard alongside the mutation and confirming the suite then goes red.

When replacing a broken safety predicate with a tested module, the module tests are only half the job: the CALLER that consumes the verdict is where the fail-open usually survives. On PCO-349 the predicate had ten passing tests while three mutations of the runbook bash that calls it -- inverting the ok comparison, deleting the module invocation outright, and misspelling the park reason -- all left the full suite green. Extract the caller (even when it is bash embedded in markdown that nothing executes in production) and drive it end to end through the real module with a stubbed outer dependency, asserting the terminal state, not just that it did not crash. Also test the DEGRADED paths explicitly: a caller can fail closed and still be wrong if an infrastructure failure is indistinguishable from not-ready-yet, because the operator then waits out the full timeout instead of seeing a diagnosable reason.

MUST-CHECK: this repo's committed tsconfig.json sets types:["bun-types"] but package.json declares zero devDependencies (no bun-types, no @types/node) and node_modules starts empty -- bunx tsc --noEmit fails at the very first line (TS2688 cannot find bun-types) on a totally clean checkout of main, before any story-specific code exists. Confirmed via git worktree add of main with the same failure. bun add is also blocked in this sandboxed environment (PermissionDenied writing to tempdir, even with the sandbox-disable flag) so the normal fix is not available inside an agent session. Workaround used: curl the bun-types and @types/node tarballs directly from the npm registry and extract them by hand into node_modules/, then typecheck with a scratch tsconfig.check.json (types:["bun-types","node"], extends the real one) to get a real signal, deleting the scratch file and the manually-fetched packages afterward since they are not part of the declared dependency set. Remaining errors under that setup (Response.text() not on type, one pre-existing stderr-property mismatch in coderabbit.test.ts) are identical on baseline main and are NOT introduced by any story -- do not mistake them for new failures. A future story fixing this properly should add bun-types + @types/node to package.json devDependencies for real, but that is a repo-tooling fix, not something to slip into an unrelated story.

When two refusal reasons are logically entailed by each other given an earlier assertion already passed (e.g. repo==projectDirRemote required to pass assertion 1, then separately checking projectDirRemote==envDirRemote and repo==envDirRemote), whichever of the two entailed checks runs SECOND becomes permanently unreachable dead code once the first assertion has already been validated as true -- the two conditions collapse into the same fact. Fix: evaluate both entailed checks BEFORE the assertion that would force them together, not after. Concretely in ship-config.ts validateShipConfig: fetch both projectDir and envDir remotes up front, check path-equality, then same-remote, then repo==envDir-remote, and ONLY THEN check repo==projectDir-remote (repo_mismatch) -- reordered from the Locked-18 assertion numbering (which lists repo-match as assertion 1) specifically so project_dir_same_remote_as_env_dir and repo_is_env_dir_remote both stay independently testable. Written up because a reviewer following the assertion numbering literally would reintroduce the dead-code trap.

MUST-CHECK: when writing a plugin.test.ts absence-assertion for text just removed from a shipped runbook (e.g. asserting Locked-17 removed a dirname "$PWD" probe and .drawbar/memory probing), do not describe the removed mechanism in the replacement comment using the EXACT literal substring the test greps for -- an explanatory comment like 'There is no dirname "$PWD" probe anymore' left inside the shipped doc trips the very test written to prove its absence. Also: a legitimate downstream reference to the same substring (e.g. KB="$ENV_DIR/.drawbar/memory", a correct derivation, not a probe) means a blanket not.toContain(".drawbar/memory") is too broad and produces a false failure -- anchor the absence assertion on the specific REMOVED CONSTRUCT (e.g. a regex for [ -d "$PWD/.drawbar/memory" ]-shaped existence checks, or the word "dirname") and explicitly assert the ONE legitimate remaining reference is still present, rather than banning the substring outright.

MUST-CHECK: two real bash bugs caught only by actually spawning the extracted fence (not by reading it): (1) mapfile/readarray require bash 4+, but macOS ships /bin/bash 3.2.57 as the FIRST bash on PATH on real developer machines -- any shipped runbook fence must use a portable `while IFS= read -r x; do ...; done < <(producer)` instead. (2) `test-condition && { echo msg; exit 1; }` (as opposed to the house style `test-condition || { echo msg; exit 1; }`) leaves the exit status of the enclosing loop/fence as the FAILED test's status (1) on every iteration where the guarded condition legitimately does NOT fire, because `&&` short-circuits without running anything and that failed test becomes the last-executed command. Harmless when more commands follow in the same fence (they overwrite $?), but a landmine for (a) any isolated/extracted-fragment test harness that treats the fragment as a whole script, and (b) any future refactor that moves the loop to the end of the fence. Always write refusal guards in the `positive-condition || { ...; exit 1; }` form used throughout scripts/lib/coderabbit.ts and commands/drawbar-ship.md, never `negative-condition && { ...; exit 1; }`, so the guard resolves to exit 0 on its own on the success path. Both bugs were caught by writing a real regression test that spawns the actual extracted bash and asserts the exit code -- neither would have been caught by reading the diff.

MUST-CHECK: a regression test for de-hardcoding (e.g. `[ x = "$VAR" ]` replacing `[ x = "literal" ]`) is invisible to a mutation that re-hardcodes the literal if every fixture pins $VAR to that same literal value. A hardcoded and a parameterized check are behaviorally identical whenever the fixture happens to match the old constant. The discriminating test must set the variable to something other than the previously-hardcoded value (e.g. BASE_BRANCH="trunk" instead of "main") and assert both directions: passes when it matches, refuses when it does not.

MUST-CHECK: never run git stash, even briefly to compare pre-fix vs post-fix doc text for a RED demonstration. Reverting one file back to HEAD to observe a test fail, then stash-popping to restore, still violates the never-git-stash constraint and risks losing uncommitted work if the pop conflicts. Use git show HEAD:<path> to read the prior committed version instead, or temporarily Edit the file and Edit it back using the exact text already captured via Read.

Node/Bun path.resolve() already normalizes away trailing slashes (resolve("/a/b/") === resolve("/a/b")). A separate stripTrailingSlash() helper applied AFTER resolve() is dead code — it can never observe a trailing slash since resolve() already removed it. Verify with node -e before adding a fixture test for a helper like this; if resolve() already covers it, delete the helper instead of pinning it with a redundant test.

MUST-CHECK vacuous-assertion-needs-preseed-state, applied to a shell variable rather than a file: when a markdown runbook has multiple bash fences meant to run as SEPARATE tool invocations (no shared shell state), a guard test that always pre-seeds the variable (e.g. RESOLVED=... prepended to every test script) can never catch the case where that variable is genuinely unset in production. Write at least one test that omits the assignment entirely (Bun.spawn env fully replaces the child env, so omitting a key reliably leaves it unset) rather than assigning it empty.

A .gitignore pattern containing a / (other than a trailing one) is anchored to the directory of the .gitignore file, not matched at every depth. ".drawbar/ship.config.json" only ignores that path at the repo root; sub/.drawbar/ship.config.json is NOT ignored. Verify with git check-ignore -v <path> against a nested path, not just the root one. Use a leading **/ to match at any depth.

MUST-CHECK: [ "$var" != "0" ] is the fail-OPEN direction when $var can be empty (e.g. an upstream command failed and produced no output) -- empty string != "0" is true, so a degraded/failed read is silently treated as success. The fail-closed form requires a genuine positive numeric result (case pattern matching empty/non-numeric explicitly, or [ "$var" -gt 0 ] after that check) and a distinct could-not-be-read message so a transient infra failure is diagnosable rather than conflated with a real pass.

MUST-CHECK vacuous-assertion-needs-preseed-state has a second, independent route besides the unset/empty-variable case: a variable can be genuinely non-empty (passing an [ -n "$VAR" ] assert) yet still carry no usable data for the downstream loop -- e.g. RESOLVED set to an empty JSON array, valid JSON missing the expected key, or malformed/non-JSON text. Each of these must be covered by its own regression test (reusing the same extraction harness, not hand-reimplemented), because a test suite that only pre-seeds well-formed JSON with a populated array can never observe this class of gap even when the guard code is already correct.

When de-hardcoding a workspace-specific literal (e.g. a Linear status name) throughout a command doc, check the YAML frontmatter description field too -- it is the one line users actually see in a plugin command list, is easy to miss because it is outside the body prose that usually gets the careful de-hardcode pass, and is cheap to pin with a regression test against the frontmatter() parser already used by command-frontmatter tests.

MUST-CHECK: jq's length builtin is defined on EVERY JSON type, not just arrays. `{"requiredChecks":"build"} | .requiredChecks | length` returns 5 (string char count), which satisfies a digits-only case guard even though `.requiredChecks[]` then errors ("Cannot iterate over string") and emits nothing, so a downstream while-loop runs zero times and exits 0 -- a vacuous pass reached by a route a count-only check never sees. Always assert `(X|type) == "array"` before trusting a length-derived count as a non-vacuity guard, and pair it with a post-loop reconciliation (count actual iterations, compare to the expected count) to close the class independently of the type guard.

MUST-CHECK: when a bash fence in a doc is a SEPARATE invocation from an earlier one (nothing carries a plain shell assignment across two Bash tool calls), the re-declare-and-assert discipline must be applied to EVERY variable the later fence consumes that originated in the earlier one -- not just the one that happens to already have a MUST-CHECK comment. Grep the later fence for every $VAR it reads and cross-check each against the earlier fence's derivation; a partially-applied fix (e.g. RESOLVED re-declared and asserted, but REPO/BASE_BRANCH silently assumed from ambient env) reopens the exact class of bug the original fix closed, and is easy to miss because the fence looks fixed at a glance.

MUST-CHECK: when tests extract a bash fence slice from a markdown doc via txt.indexOf("literal command text"), adding a NEW comment elsewhere in the same fence that happens to quote that same literal text (e.g. explaining why a later step needs a variable, and mentioning the exact command that consumes it) can shift indexOf to the wrong occurrence and silently break or corrupt an unrelated extraction helper. Always grep the whole file for any literal string used as a test extraction anchor before adding prose that might repeat it, and re-run the full test file (not just the tests you just touched) after any doc edit.

MUST-CHECK: when a story constraint says No git stash, do not reach for git stash even briefly to get a genuine RED run against the pre-fix source. Use a manual substitute instead: copy the current (fixed) file aside, overwrite the working file with git show HEAD:path, run the test, then restore from the manual copy. It never touches the stash ref and cannot collide with any stash the user has in flight. Caught this mid-session via the system's file-change reminder after one git stash push/pop round-trip; no work was lost, but the constraint should be honored from the first RED, not just after a slip.

MUST-CHECK: a mutation gate is only as trustworthy as the specificity of the assertions it relies on. Two separate guards in the same shell fence can emit different FATAL messages that share a token (e.g. both mention the same variable name), so a test asserting only `output contains "<VAR>"` still passes when the guard it is named after is deleted — the OTHER guard fires and satisfies the substring. The gate then reports CAUGHT for a mutant that actually survives, which is worse than no gate because it manufactures confidence. Same failure shape for a negative doc assertion over-fitted to one byte sequence: asserting a file does not contain a specific markdown-emphasised string is defeated by re-introducing the same literal with different emphasis, while a companion positive assertion stays satisfied by an unrelated occurrence elsewhere in the section. Two rules: assert the exact, unique message text a guard emits, and pair every negative absence assertion with a POSITIVE anchor on the instruction line that must be present. Verify the gate itself by confirming each mutation fails the test NAMED for it, not merely that some test failed.

MUST-CHECK: `jq "X | length"` is defined for every JSON type, not just arrays — length of a string is its character count and length of a number is its magnitude. So a digits-only vacuity guard over `X | length` PASSES for a scalar, and the following `X[]` iteration then errors, emits nothing, and a `while read` loop over it runs zero times while exiting 0. In a shell fence that gates a destructive step, that is a silent fall-through with no output and no refusal — the exact failure the count guard was written to prevent, reached through a different payload shape. This is live wherever the JSON is hand-carried between two separate shell invocations by an agent, since re-serialising a one-element array as a bare scalar is a routine paste error. Fix BOTH halves: assert `(X|type) == "array"` before trusting length, and independently reconcile work actually done against the expected count after the loop (`[ "$verified" -eq "$EXPECTED" ]`), which also catches a jq or upstream process that dies part-way through the list. Enumerating one more bad shape per bug report does not converge; the reconciliation closes the whole class.

MUST-CHECK: when a runbook assigns shell variables in one fenced code block and consumes them in another, nothing carries the assignment across — each fence is a separate process. Fixing this for the ONE variable a bug report named is the common half-fix: audit every variable the second fence CONSUMES and re-derive all of them from a single re-declared source of truth, then run the same non-empty/not-null assert loop over the whole set. The dangerous ones are those that fail closed only by accident (an empty repo slug making a CLI call error, so the guard passes for the wrong reason and reports a misleading cause) and those whose names are commonly exported in an operator shell (REPO, BRANCH, PR) — an ambient value is then silently trusted and every downstream call, including the destructive one, targets the wrong resource. Test with an UNSEEDED harness: if every fixture pre-seeds the variable as a convenience, no test can ever see the gap. Add at least one fixture that supplies nothing but the source-of-truth payload, plus one that sets a deliberately poisoned ambient value and asserts the derived value wins.

When a downstream schema (run-state.ts resolved_config) embeds an already-validated upstream shape (ship-config.ts ResolvedConfig = ShipConfig + observed), validate the embedded part by re-stringifying the candidate object and calling the upstream parseX(text) function rather than hand-copying its field checks. Keeps the two validators from drifting; only the added fields (observed) need their own structural check.

To prove a guard genuinely short-circuits before a side-effecting action (e.g. duplicate-dispatch guard), inject the action as a runner function and assert a call-counter array is empty, not just that the return value looks like a no-op. A verdict object alone can be right for the wrong reason if the side-effecting call happened anyway.

MUST-CHECK: the repo leak-regression rule for issue ids is /\b(?!PCO-)[A-Z]{2,6}-\d{2,}\b/ -- it only matches an UPPERCASE team-prefix shape. Test fixtures needing story-id-shaped placeholders (e.g. to reproduce an invoked_as-carries-a-story-id defect) can safely use lowercase forms like "story-a" -- verify with node (not grep -E, which lacks lookahead support for the negative-lookahead clause) before trusting a fixture is scrub-safe.

To get a genuine RED run for a second batch of tests against an already-partially-implemented module (without git stash, which is forbidden), cp the current full implementation to a scratch path, truncate/edit the working file to remove just the not-yet-tested section, run the tests to see the real failure, then cp the scratch copy back. Confirms the RED is real (missing export/behavior) rather than a typo, without touching git state.

A duplicate-dispatch guard (write a claim record, then act) is only a real guard if the claim is DURABLE before the action fires. Structuring the function as act-then-return-state-for-caller-to-persist has two failure modes: (a) if building the claim record throws (e.g. new Date(invalidNow).toISOString() on a NaN input), it throws AFTER the action already ran, so the action fired with no claim ever persisted; (b) if the action itself throws, the claim-carrying return value never reaches the caller, so it is never persisted either. Both leave the next invocation free to dispatch a genuine duplicate. Fix: build the claim state first (refusing outright, before any side effect, if inputs are invalid rather than letting a throw happen after the fact), call an injected persist(state) writer with it, THEN fire the action. Test the ordering directly with a shared call-log array asserting persist appears before the action, and a case where the action throws but persist was already called.

MUST-CHECK: when a pure verdict function compares now-timestamp against N*configuredThreshold to decide stale-vs-fresh, an unvalidated threshold is a live defect in TWO opposite directions depending on its degraded value, not one: threshold<=0 (from Number(""), a jq // empty miss, or an unset config field) makes a genuinely fresh/live state compare as stale -> fail-open into whatever the stale branch does (e.g. spins up a second concurrent actor), while threshold=NaN makes the comparison always false -> the state can never be judged stale -> permanent deadlock. Exporting a validator function is not the fix; it must be CALLED at every comparison site, including pure functions a test or caller can invoke directly while bypassing the CLI/parse boundary. The correct response to an invalid threshold is neither of the two existing verdict branches (no_op or crash_recovery/stale) -- pick a THIRD, explicitly named refusal so an invalid config is diagnosable and never silently mistaken for a real state judgment.

MUST-CHECK: a staleness escape hatch (now - recordedAt > threshold -> route to recovery) is only reachable if recordedAt actually parses to a finite instant. A parser that accepts any non-empty string for a timestamp field lets Date.parse(v) return NaN downstream; NaN compared against a numeric threshold is always false, so the record looks permanently fresh and the escape hatch that exists specifically to prevent a deadlock becomes itself unreachable. A future-dated timestamp has the same failure shape via a different route: a negative elapsed value never exceeds a positive staleness threshold either. Fix in both places: validate parseability (Number.isFinite(Date.parse(v))) with its own named rejection reason at the PARSE boundary, AND re-validate independently inside the pure verdict function itself, because callers (including tests) can construct the record directly and skip the parser. Treat an unparseable or implausibly-future-dated timestamp as its own distinct verdict that routes TOWARD recovery, never toward the same no-op branch a healthy fresh record takes.

MUST-CHECK: as the verifying lead, do not accept a green test for a safety-guard acceptance criterion as evidence the criterion is met. An AC of the form 'a stale/degraded state routes to recovery' is typically tested with ONE well-formed degraded fixture, which passes, while an input the parser separately ADMITS makes the recovery branch unreachable in production -- the AC's stated test is green and its entire purpose is defeated. Concretely on PCO-350: parseRunState admitted any non-empty string as a timestamp, so Date.parse returned NaN downstream, NaN > threshold is always false, and the staleness escape whose written rationale was 'otherwise a crashed run deadlocks every later invocation' produced exactly that deadlock forever -- with 373 tests green. The lead-side habit that catches this: for every guard AC, hand-probe the DEGRADED path (unparseable, empty, negative, zero, NaN, future-dated, absent-vs-null) with a throwaway bun -e script against the real module before starting review, and ask in which direction each degraded value fails. Ask it in BOTH directions -- the same unvalidated threshold that deadlocks on NaN fails OPEN on 0, dispatching a duplicate agent against a live one. Independently found by the lead and both reviewers here, which is also evidence the dual-review split is doing real work rather than duplicating one reviewer.

MUST-CHECK: a path-segment validator that blocks /, \, and .. still admits every control character, including a literal newline, unless it explicitly rejects them too (e.g. /[\x00-\x1f\x7f]/). A field that is both interpolated into a filesystem path AND carried into agent-facing prose (a re-dispatch brief, a Linear comment) turns an embedded newline into a path-shape vector and a prompt-injection vector at the same time -- reviewers checking only slash/traversal shapes will miss this. Fix at the single shared string-validation primitive (e.g. isNonEmptyString) rather than only the one field a report happened to name, so every other field built on the same primitive (story ids, array entries fed into the same downstream sinks) is closed by the same change, and add a positive test asserting the exact reported payload (not just an abstract control-char fixture) is now rejected.

MUST-CHECK: a test that asserts a runbook/markdown doc still contains a required instruction must normalize whitespace before matching (e.g. section.replace(/\s+/g, " ")), never assert a literal string spanning a newline. Prose paragraphs are hard-wrapped, so which words land on which line is an editorial accident: an assertion like toContain("in_flight:\nnull") passes only while the wrap happens to fall between those two tokens and goes RED on an ordinary reflow that changed nothing about what the doc instructs -- a false failure that trains people to weaken the assertion. Same principle as keying a duplicate-implementation scan on trimmed line CONTENT rather than line number: assert on content, never on position or formatting. Verify a doc-grep guard in three directions before trusting it, not one: (1) delete the instruction it guards -> must go RED; (2) reflow the paragraph without changing meaning -> must stay GREEN; (3) baseline -> GREEN. Direction (2) is the one usually skipped, and it is what distinguishes a guard from a tripwire on the formatter.

PCO-351 (S6, updated fix pass 2): commands/drawbar-ship.md section 4 no longer implements identity/base/state/checks/config-diff itself. It delegates the ENTIRE pre-merge verdict to one `bun run .../merge-guard.ts verdict` invocation (stdin JSON {resolvedConfig, snapshot, configPath}, flags --repo/--pr/--story), fails closed on {non-zero module exit, unparseable/empty stdout, non-ok verdict}, then runs gh pr merge, then a second `merge-guard.ts record-merge-sha` call (flags --repo/--pr/--base/--dir) captures/asserts the merge_sha, anchored via `git -C <dir>` (Critical A fix pass 2 — never the ambient CWD). A new SNAPSHOT env var had to be added to the fence (re-declared like RESOLVED) since section 4 previously never had access to the T0 snapshot array at all. `configPath` (Critical 3c) and PROJECT_DIR/`--dir` (Critical A) were added to the stdin/CLI contract in the fix pass that followed the initial extraction.

PCO-351 (S6) resolved run-state.ts's forward-pointing MERGE_SHA_SHAPE comment: parseRunState's PARSE-time shape stays permissive (/^[0-9a-f]{7,40}$/) so it can still read the two legacy run-state files with abbreviated shas. The strict 40-char, merge-commit-not-head-sha assertion (Locked 10) is owned exclusively by merge-guard.ts's recordMergeSha, the one call site that ever WRITES a fresh merge_sha. Do not tighten run-state.ts's parser without first migrating legacy files, or parseRunState will start refusing state it must still read.

MUST-CHECK: when adding a new file to plugin.test.ts's leak-regression scan NEW_PUBLIC_FILES list, the comment explaining WHY it's safe can itself trip the very rule it's justifying if it quotes an unsafe example fixture id (a 2+-digit team-prefixed id written literally inside a comment in plugin.test.ts itself matched the issue-id regex). Also: explanatory prose describing a guard (e.g. a sentence saying a fence must never fall back silently on a degraded read) can itself contain the literal forbidden substring if phrased carelessly. Always re-run the leak-scan/self-referential test after adding such comments, not just the feature tests.

MUST-CHECK: when extracting a bash guard into a tested module, diff the OLD guard clause-by-clause against the NEW one before deleting the old tests — merge-guard.ts (PCO-351 S6) dropped the global fail/cancel/pending gate that used to sit above the requiredChecks loop, and its anti-vacuity check lost its bucket constraint, both silently, because nothing enumerated the source bash guard's clauses against the new implementation's. A PR with failing CI merged clean under the extracted version. Enumerate every branch of the ORIGINAL guard as a checklist and tick each one off against the new module's test suite before deleting the old bash/tests.

MUST-CHECK: gh pr diff --name-only (and plain git diff --name-only) shows only the DESTINATION path of a rename, never the source, once similarity is >=50%% (a rename-with-modification still counts). A file-identity guard (e.g. refusing a diff that touches a specific config file) must read the files API (gh api repos/<repo>/pulls/<pr>/files, exposing .filename AND .previous_filename) instead, or a rename hides the file from --name-only entirely. Also match basenames case-insensitively (darwin is case-insensitive) and against the actually-resolved effective path, not only a hardcoded default basename.

A `VAR=$(module ...)` command substitution captures the module's stdout into VAR, but VAR itself never leaves that single Bash tool invocation — a later step's instructions to "record $VAR" are directions to a shell variable in a FINISHED process, not a usable value. If a later step (a different Bash call, or prose read by an agent) needs the captured value, the fence must explicitly `echo "key=$VAR"` so it lands on stdout the caller can actually see. commands/drawbar-ship.md captured $MERGE_SHA via command substitution and never echoed it, so step 5's instruction to record it was undeliverable.

MUST-CHECK: an injected Runner (git/gh spawn wrapper) with no explicit cwd/`-C` silently inherits whatever directory the calling process happens to be in. A post-merge guard (e.g. ancestry assertion via `git merge-base --is-ancestor`) that depends on this without an explicit `-C <dir>` anchor will run against the wrong checkout on every invocation, and if the guard sits AFTER an irreversible step (like `gh pr merge`), the failure mode is a permanent post-hoc refusal, not a caught bug. Always thread an explicit, validated absolute directory through the injected-runner seam rather than relying on ambient CWD.

MUST-CHECK: a paginated REST API endpoint with an undocumented-in-error-form server-side item cap (e.g. GitHub's list-PR-files endpoint capping at 3000 entries) truncates SILENTLY once the cap is hit — exit 0 / HTTP 200, a short list, simply no further pagination Link header. A CLI pagination flag (like `gh ... --paginate`) will not surface this as an error. Any security-relevant scan built on such a list (e.g. scanning changed files for a sensitive path) must independently verify the TOTAL count against a separate, capped-differently field (e.g. `changedFiles` from a different endpoint) before trusting the list is complete.

merge-guard.ts's mergeVerdict refuses on ANY check (not just a requiredChecks entry) still sitting at bucket "pending" (reason checks_still_pending). This is a DELIBERATE tightening beyond the bash this module replaced (which only gated fail/cancel, never pending) — not a restoration of prior behavior, despite an earlier comment incorrectly claiming provenance from the old bash. Rationale: a required check that is pending is already caught by required_check_missing; this gate exists specifically to cover a NON-required check still pending, on the theory that an unresolved CI signal anywhere is worth blocking on. Accepted trade-off: a permanently-pending, non-required check (misconfigured or simply slow) deadlocks /drawbar-ship until it resolves — judged an acceptable risk in this workspace. Do not weaken this gate, and do not re-attribute it to the old bash in future comments.

MUST-CHECK: when a test extracts a runnable script out of a markdown doc by slicing at a literal marker (e.g. block.indexOf("gh pr merge -R")), that exact string must appear EXACTLY ONCE in the block. Writing it again inside an explanatory comment ABOVE the real command silently truncates every extracted fence at the comment instead, so the tests execute a short script that stops before the logic under test - and they go GREEN, because a script that ends early exits 0. Caught only because an unrelated assertion expected a non-zero exit. Two defenses: assert the marker occurs exactly once before slicing, and when documenting the command in a comment, describe it in prose rather than reproducing its literal invocation.

MUST-CHECK: handing a filesystem path that came from agent-writable state (a run-state file, a cached payload) to git -C is an arbitrary-code-execution sink, not merely a wrong-directory bug. A repository whose .git configuration an attacker controls executes commands on an ordinary read: core.sshCommand fires on any fetch against an ssh-form remote, and the reference-transaction hook fires on a successful one (both reproduced on git 2.50.1). An absolute-path-and-no-dotdot check does NOT help - it constrains the shape of the path, never WHOSE repository it names. The trust root for such a path must be a file no agent writes (the operator-authored config), with the mutable copy required to AGREE with it rather than being used directly. Corollary for re-deriving a value to break a tautology: if the new observation is anchored at a path taken from the same untrusted object, the tautology just moved one indirection deeper - coordinated tampering of both fields still passes.

When asserting the allowed module set in scripts/lib/, never assert a literal count (e.g. length === 5 or === 9) — the epic-added set (coderabbit.ts, ship-config.ts, run-state.ts, merge-guard.ts, kb-sync.ts) lands incrementally across stories, so a literal count is wrong the moment one module has not yet landed (kb-sync.ts, as of PCO-352). Instead assert every module on disk (readdirSync, never hardcoded) is a member of the union of a PRE_EXISTING set (predates the epic) and an EPIC_ADDED set (the five), and separately assert each EPIC_ADDED module present has a co-located *.test.ts.

MUST-CHECK: when slicing a markdown section from commands/drawbar-ship.md for content assertions in scripts/plugin.test.ts, normalize whitespace (collapse runs of whitespace to a single space) before asserting toContain on multi-word phrases. Markdown hard-wraps prose at roughly 80 columns, so a phrase like 'Re-sort and continue' can land as 'Re-sort and' then a line break then 'continue' in the raw slice, making a correct toContain assertion fail for a formatting reason, not a content reason. The established section() helper elsewhere in plugin.test.ts already normalizes; new slice helpers should follow that convention rather than hand-rolling regex with embedded optional-newline escapes.

MUST-CHECK: when a rule has clauses with DIFFERENT outcomes (some clear a condition, one asks the agent to re-pick/retry instead), never put them all under one header like "satisfied if any of the following clauses holds" — an agent under time pressure resolves that ambiguity toward the cheap reading (gate satisfied, proceed) even for the clause that actually means "your pick was wrong, redo it." Mark the outcome-differing clause explicitly (e.g. "(re-pick, not a clearance)") both in the clause itself and in the header/intro, and give it a terminator condition if it can re-fire (a re-sort-and-retry clause needs an explicit halt when the re-sort does not change the outcome, or it livelocks on a state left by a crash mid-run).

MUST-CHECK: when a rule resolves a merge commit sha for story X by scanning a persisted map/list (e.g. a run-state file's merged{} map, or a gh pr list --search result), an unkeyed scan over every entry's sha is a silent pass generator — since any commit already on the base branch is trivially an ancestor of itself, ANY story ever merged supplies a passing sha for an ancestry check on ANY other story. Require an exact-key lookup (merged[<id>], never merged[*].merge_sha), and on a gh-search route require exactly one result matching both the target ref (baseRefName) and the id as a whole token (never substring/prefix) — refuse on zero or multiple matches, since --search is full-text and a short id can prefix-match a longer one.

MUST-CHECK: pinning tests for prose runbooks (toContain assertions on doc slices) that were only verified by deleting the target sentence miss a whole mutation class: DEMOTING a hard conjunct to a parenthetical aside ("X and Y" -> "X (Y, normally) -- optionally...") or WEAKENING a qualifier ("an unsatisfied blocker" -> "a blocker") leaves every token-level toContain assertion green, since the tokens still appear somewhere in the slice. Fix: pin the exact conjoined/qualified PHRASE as one contiguous string (post whitespace-normalization), not just its constituent tokens checked independently. Verify by both deleting AND rewording the target during development (temporarily edit the doc, rerun, confirm the specific new test fails, then revert) -- deletion alone is not sufficient mutation coverage.

MUST-CHECK: never cite a line number of the SAME file you are editing (e.g. "see `:329-337`"). The edit that adds the citation usually also inserts lines above its own target, so the citation is stale the moment it is written — observed on PCO-352, where a fix pass cited `:329-337` and `:352-358` while its own ~100 inserted lines pushed both targets ~60 lines down. Cite a stable textual anchor instead (a heading, a named fence marker, a unique comment string). The same hazard applies one step out to CROSS-file line citations into modules the same epic is actively editing, and it is made worse by pinning the citation in a test: the range then cannot rot silently, but it also cannot be corrected without touching the test, and a reviewer reads the green test as evidence the citation is right.

MUST-CHECK: a rule that must GATHER EVIDENCE from external tools (git, gh, an API) cannot be specified safely in prose, even when a locked decision correctly says the surrounding rule must stay prose. On PCO-352 the blocker gate legitimately stays prose (Linear blockedBy relations are not machine-readable, so a TS module would get an empty edge set and be fail-open vacuous) — but ONE of its four clauses required proving a merge commit is an ancestor of the base branch. That single clause accumulated SEVEN Criticals across two review rounds (unanchored gh/git calls resolving against the wrong repo; a sha never bound to the blocker it was clearing; extraction by array index after validating a filtered predicate; a self-attesting run-state route preferred over the authoritative server-side one; a trust-root prohibition stated as prose where the executable config comparison was needed), while the other three clauses and the two unrelated deliverables in the same story stayed clean through both rounds. The distinguishing property is not "safety-critical" but "needs a multi-step evidence protocol with anchoring, binding, precedence and failure semantics" — prose has no place to put those, and every fix pass rewrites them slightly differently. Lead-side rule: when review findings concentrate in ONE clause of a rule rather than spreading, that clause is a separate story, not a fix-pass item — split it out, land the clean remainder, and pin the ABSENCE of the deferred clause with a test plus a written reason so a later reader does not hand-write a substitute.

kb-sync.ts syncKnowledge applies the report's lessons[] via appendEntry ONCE, before the retry loop starts -- not on every attempt. The retry loop's per-attempt work is re-staging/committing/rebasing/pushing what is ALREADY on disk (including any inline drawbar-kb add writes and the just-applied lessons); re-invoking appendEntry per attempt would be harmless (idempotent) but adds nothing, since appendEntry's own semantics already make a repeat call a no-op.

When a retry loop stages files that may not exist yet (e.g. knowledge.archive.jsonl, only created on a supersede), the existence check must be re-evaluated INSIDE the loop on every attempt, not cached once before it -- otherwise a file that appears mid-run (during the backoff sleep) is never picked up by a later attempt's git add. Caught by a test that injects the file-creation side effect into the injected sleep() seam itself, simulating a concurrent write landing during the backoff window.

MUST-CHECK: any edit to commands/drawbar-ship.md (or agents/drawbar-story-lead.md) that introduces a NEW word-word or id-id pair joined by a single slash (e.g. S8/PCO-353, story-lead/implementer) trips scripts/plugin.test.ts's owner/repo GitHub-slug leak-scan rule, which scans every line for a slug-shaped pattern. Reword to avoid the slash (e.g. S8, PCO-353 or story-lead or implementer) rather than widening the reviewed ALLOWLIST, unless the pair is genuinely going to recur across many future edits.

MUST-CHECK: when the same guard shape appears at TWO call sites (e.g. the identical `status --porcelain --untracked-files=no` precondition in both a sync loop and its preflight function), mutation-testing only one site proves nothing about the other. Caught in PCO-353: deleting the flag from the sync-side call killed a test, deleting it from the preflight-side call left the suite fully green -- 0 failed / 39 ran. The behaviour was correct and a real-git probe confirmed it, so this was a pure test-coverage hole, invisible to a green suite and to a reviewer reading the diff (both call sites LOOK identically guarded, because they are). Enumerate every occurrence of a repeated guard (grep the literal argv/flag) and mutate each one independently. Corollary: a surviving mutant on a guard whose behaviour is demonstrably correct is still worth closing -- it is the test that is missing, so the fix is a red-green on the TEST, not on the module.

MUST-CHECK: a module built on Locked-5 injected runners is fully testable with the tool absent from PATH -- and therefore CANNOT validate any assumption it makes about the REAL tool argv semantics or output format. Every such assumption is asserted only against a fake the same author wrote, so a wrong assumption is green in the suite and broken in production. In PCO-353 kb-sync.ts these were: `git diff --cached --quiet` exiting 1 (not 2/128) when something is staged; `git check-attr merge -- <path>` printing exactly `<path>: merge: union` and `unspecified` for an uncovered path; and above all whether a REAL `git push` rejection stderr matches the retry-classification regexes -- if it did not, every rejection would be misclassified as a hard failure and the tolerant retry loop would never retry once, silently. As the verifying lead, spend the few minutes to build a throwaway real fixture (bare remote + two clones, GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL pointed at a scratch file so the operator config is untouched) and drive the actual CLI through the real divergence. All four assumptions held here, but none of them were PROVEN by the 39 green unit tests.
